heath_proof: Let ABC be a circle, and let a point D be taken outside ABC; let there be drawn through from it straight lines DA, DE, DF, DC, and let DA be through the centre; I say that, of the straight lines falling on the concave circumference AEFC, the straight line DA through the centre is greatest, while DE is greater than DF and DF than DC.; but, of the straight lines falling on the convex circumference HLKG, the straight line DG between the point and the diameter AG is least; and the nearer to the least DG is always less than the more remote, namely DK than DL, and DL than DH. For let the centre of the circle ABC be taken [III. 1], and let it be M; let ME, MF, MC, MK, ML, MH be joined. Then, since AM is equal to EM, let MD be added to each; therefore AD is equal to EM, MD. But EM, MD are greater than ED; [I. 20] therefore AD is also greater than ED. Again, since ME is equal to MF, and MD is common, therefore EM, MD are equal to FM, MD; and the angle EMD is greater than the angle FMD;  therefore the base ED is greater than the base FD. [I. 24]  Similarly we can prove that FD is greater than CD; therefore DA is greatest, while DE is greater than DF, and DF than DC. Next, since MK, KD are greater than MD, [I. 20] and MG is equal to MK, therefore the remainder KD is greater than the remainder GD, so that GD is less than KD. And, since on MD, one of the sides of the triangle MLD, two straight lines MK, KD were constructed meeting within the triangle, therefore MK, KD are less than ML, LD; [I. 21] and MK is equal to ML; therefore the remainder DK is less than the remainder DL. Similarly we can prove that DL is also less than DH; therefore DG is least, while DK is less than DL, and DL than DH. I say also that only two equal straight lines will fall from the point D on the circle, one on each side of the least DG. On the straight line MD, and at the point M on it, let the angle DMB be constructed equal to the angle KMD, and let DB be joined. Then, since MK is equal to MB, and MD is common, the two sides KM, MD are equal to the two sides BM, MD respectively; and the angle KMD is equal to the angle BMD; therefore the base DK is equal to the base DB. [I. 4]  I say that no other straight line equal to the straight line DK will fall on the circle from the point D. For, if possible, let a straight line so fall, and let it be DN. Then, since DK is equal to DN,   while DK is equal to DB, DB is also equal to DN, that is, the nearer to the least DG equal to the more remote: which was proved impossible. Therefore no more than two equal straight lines will fall on the circle ABC from the point D, one on each side of DG the least.
ai_proof_text:
3.8
**Statement:** If a point be taken outside a circle and from the point straight lines be drawn through to the circle, one of which is through the centre and the others are drawn at random, then, of the straight lines which fall on the concave circumference, that through the centre is greatest, while of the rest   the nearer to that through the centre is always greater than the more remote, but, of the straight lines falling on the convex circumference, that between the point and the diameter is least, while of the rest the nearer to the least is always less than the more remote, and only two equal straight lines will fall on the circle from the point, one on each side of the least.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a circle and D a point taken outside it. From D let straight lines DA, DE, DF, DC be drawn through to the circle, DA through the centre and the others at random, so that they meet the concave circumference at A, E, F, C and the convex circumference at G, K, L, H respectively (G on DA, K on DE, L on DF, H on DC), the lines lying on one side of DA with DE nearer to DA than DF, and DF nearer than DC. Let the centre M of the circle ABC be taken [3.1]; M lies on the straight line DA between G and A, so that DA is DM together with MA, and DM is DG together with GM. Join ME, MF, MC, MK, ML, MH [P1].

**Step 2.** (DA is the greatest of the straight lines falling on the concave circumference.) In the triangle EMD the two sides EM, MD are together greater than ED [1.20]. But EM is equal to AM, both being radii of the circle [D1.15]; therefore AM, MD together are greater than ED. But AM, MD together are the whole DA, since M lies on DA. Therefore DA is greater than DE. In the same manner DA is greater than DF and than DC, and than every straight line from D to the concave circumference; therefore DA is the greatest.

**Step 3.** (Of the rest, the nearer to DA is greater than the more remote.) In the triangles EMD, FMD the side EM is equal to the side FM [D1.15], MD is common, and, since DE is nearer to the line through the centre than DF, the angle EMD is greater than the angle FMD. Therefore, two sides being equal to two sides and the included angle greater, the base ED is greater than the base FD [1.24]. In the same manner, in the triangles FMD, CMD, FM is equal to CM, MD is common, and the angle FMD is greater than the angle CMD; therefore FD is greater than CD [1.24].

**Step 4.** (DG is the least of the straight lines falling on the convex circumference.) In the triangle MKD the two sides MK, KD are together greater than MD [1.20]. But MK is equal to MG [D1.15], and MD is MG together with GD; therefore MG, KD together are greater than MG, GD together. Let MG be subtracted from each; therefore the remainder KD is greater than the remainder GD [CN3]. Thus DG is less than DK, and in the same way DG is less than DL and than DH; therefore DG is the least.

**Step 5.** (Of the rest, the nearer to DG is less than the more remote.) Since DK is nearer to DG than DL, the point K falls within the triangle MLD, so that MK, KD are two straight lines constructed from the extremities M, D of the side MD and meeting within the triangle MLD. Therefore MK, KD together are less than the remaining two sides ML, LD together [1.21]. But MK is equal to ML [D1.15]; subtracting these equals, the remainder KD is less than the remainder LD [CN3]. In the same manner L falls within the triangle MHD, so that ML, LD together are less than MH, HD together [1.21]; and ML is equal to MH [D1.15]; therefore LD is less than HD [CN3]. Thus DK is less than DL, and DL less than DH.

**Step 6.** (Two equal straight lines fall from D on the circle, one on each side of DG.) At the point M on the straight line MD, on the other side of DA from K, let the angle DMB be constructed equal to the angle DMK [1.23], the straight line MB being terminated at the point B of the circumference, and let DB be joined [P1]. Then in the triangles KMD, BMD the side MK is equal to the side MB, both being radii [D1.15], MD is common, and the angle KMD is equal to the angle BMD; therefore the base DK is equal to the base DB [1.4]. Thus DK, DB are two equal straight lines falling from D on the circle, one on each side of the least DG.

**Step 7.** (No other straight line equal to DK falls from D on the circle.) If possible, let another straight line DN, equal to DK, fall from D on the convex circumference, N being a point different from K and from B. Since DN is equal to DK, and DK is equal to DB, DN is equal to DB [CN1]. Now N lies on one side of DG. If N lies on the same side as B, then DN, DB are two straight lines falling on the convex circumference on the same side of DG, and one of them is nearer to DG than the other; therefore by Step 5 the nearer is less than the more remote, so that DN is not equal to DB, which is absurd. If N lies on the same side as K, then in the same way DN is not equal to DK, which is absurd. Therefore no straight line other than DK, DB and equal to them falls from D on the circle, and only two equal straight lines fall on the circle from D, one on each side of the least. (The same construction and reasoning, using Step 3 in place of Step 5, gives the corresponding result for a straight line falling on the concave circumference.)
